title: 2027 Volkswagen Jetta: Prices, Reviews & Pictures - CarGurus.com
summary: Explore the 2027 Volkswagen Jetta with CarGurus reviews, pricing insights, comparisons, news and expert analysis.
body_markdown:
## Look & feel


7/10


The 2027 Volkswagen Jetta is available in S, Sport, SE, and SEL trim levels, with prices ranging from $25,320 to $31,320, including the $1,325 destination charge. Our Jetta SEL test vehicle had extra-cost Monument Gray paint and a set of all-weather floor mats, bringing the manufacturer’s suggested retail price (MSRP) to $31,945, including destination. A Jetta GLI sports sedan is also available for $35,120, but is not covered in this review.


Though the Jetta’s current design dates to the 2019 model year, Volkswagen refreshed the car in 2025, giving it a cleaner and more contemporary appearance. As we'd expect, the Jetta SEL has the most upscale look with an illuminated grille light bar, added brightwork, and attractive 18-inch wheels with a machined-finish surface. With SEL trim, buyers can get a Jetta painted in red, blue, black, white, and shades of gray.


Inside, the car’s no-nonsense design theme continues. However, the SEL’s cabin has some personality thanks to a large digital driver display, shiny surfaces and trim, and metallic accents. This version of the Jetta also comes with genuine leather upholstery in gray (Grigio) or brown (Sevilla), and a 10-color ambient lighting system adds a premium vibe after dark.


Most controls incorporate real buttons and knobs, are located where drivers would expect to find them, and are well-marked on a matte-black background. The exceptions include the infotainment screen’s touch-sensing menu shortcuts and the touch-sensing dual-zone automatic climate control panel, both of which suffer from glare and reflections.


Worse, some of the infotainment system’s on-screen controls are hidden until the driver raises a hand toward the proximity-sensing display. That’s fine when the car is parked, but it turns a one-step action into two steps on the move. The first is the hand raise that activates the hidden controls, and the second is finding and then using the desired control before the system decides to hide it again. On multiple occasions when using the infotainment system’s knobs, we also mistakenly brushed one of the touch-sensing shortcuts surrounding them, messing everything up.


The climate panel is distracting, too. Mounted low at the bottom of the dashboard underneath the air vents, drivers must look down to find the touch-sensing control they want to use, then coordinate their fingertip with the desired outcome. Knobs that drivers can feel and twist without looking away from the road are a much better solution.


## Performance


6/10


Gutless engines are commonplace in the compact car class. The Jetta’s turbocharged 1.5-liter four-cylinder is not that, providing 158 horsepower and 184 pound-feet of torque, but it suffers from such significant turbo lag that it’s almost as displeasing as a weak, naturally aspirated engine.


Step on the accelerator in Normal driving mode and not much happens. Press harder, and the torque floods in with a surge that can break the front tires loose. There are two solutions to this problem. First, just be patient. Second, switch the eight-speed automatic into Sport mode, which hastens throttle response and does a better job of keeping the engine in the thick of the torque band.


Using Sport mode makes the Jetta better to drive, but it likely also reduces fuel economy. The official EPA rating is 33 mpg combined, and we recorded 33.7 mpg on our fuel-economy evaluation route. On the mountainous testing loop, the Jetta returned 29.4 mpg, but that included some use of the Sport driving mode and unusually heavy traffic.


Unlike competitors such as the Honda Civic, the Hyundai Elantra, and the Toyota Corolla, the VW Jetta does not offer a hybrid powertrain option. It needs one to appeal to people who spend a lot of time driving in traffic and in the city, where hybrids can save significant money, and where a hybrid’s electric assist motor could erase the Jetta’s turbo lag. During our test, the Jetta mustered no better than 23.4 mpg in city and suburban driving, but we observed 41.2 mpg during a drive that was almost exclusively highway travel.


Though Volkswagen equips the racy Jetta GLI with an independent rear suspension, the rest of the lineup makes do with a simpler (and cheaper) torsion-beam setup. In all but the base S trim level, it features “sport” tuning and a 0.6-inch ride-height reduction.


In ordinary driving, the suspension feels rudimentary with a busy and sometimes brittle ride quality. Drivers will make peace with it if they convince themselves that this is the heightened state of communication inherent in driving a German car.


Run the Jetta SEL on a favorite backroad in Sport mode, and its Germanic driving character shines through. It’s not as satisfying as a Jetta GLI, of course, but the suspension deftly blends compliance and control, the steering is light and precise, the grip is good from tires that resist squealing, and clear outward sightlines make it easy to place the Jetta exactly where drivers want to. Though this front-driver’s nose can push a bit wide in tighter curves, the SEL is well balanced, predictable, secure, and trustworthy when driven with enthusiasm.


The Jetta SEL is even more at home on the open road thanks to its communicative ride, speed-sensing steering, good passing power, and comfortable driver’s seat. It’s relatively quiet inside, too.


The Jetta doesn’t offer all-wheel drive (AWD). If that's important, buyers should consider the Mazda3, the Subaru Impreza, or the Toyota Corolla LE Hybrid—the only version of Toyota’s compact that offers it.


## Form & function


9/10


The Volkswagen Jetta is an undeniably practical car, and aside from its lack of an AWD option, it’s ready for winter driving. Heated side mirrors and rain-sensing wipers are standard on every trim level, and the Jetta SEL has heated wiper-park rests, a heated steering wheel, and heated front and rear seats. The SEL also addresses muggy summer temperatures with ventilated front seats.


A height-adjustable driver’s seat is standard and power-adjustable with lumbar support in all Jettas except for the base S trim level. It is a comfortable chair, but in our SEL test car we wished for a separate adjustment to increase the angle of the seat cushion for better leg support. We appreciated the densely padded center armrest, though, and the oversized sunroof that lets in plenty of light.


Volkswagen doesn’t offer height adjustment for the front passenger’s seat. However, a passenger who frequently complains about that omission said that she didn’t feel like she was sitting on the car’s floor, so we'll chalk that up as a win for VW.


The rear seats are reasonably comfortable with good leg and knee room, softly padded front seatbacks, and in our SEL test car, heated outboard seating positions. As with the front seats, we wished the back-seat cushion offered more thigh support. Air conditioning vents and USB charging ports are missing, and the shallow cupholders in the center armrest do not look trustworthy. The coat hooks are thoughtful details, though.


Storage space in front is commendable. Under the center armrest, the storage box is thoughtfully shaped and lined at the bottom. Also, the Jetta’s glove compartment is huge, the wireless charging pad has a rubber surface that holds devices in place, and there is a slot on the center console perfect for holding the key fob. The Jetta also has an overhead sunglasses storage compartment and sizable bottle holders and storage trays in the lower door panels.


Press the trunk release on the remote key fob, and the lid pops and opens to reveal a roomy 14.1-cubic-foot trunk that’s nearly as large as a midsize Toyota Camry's. VW doesn’t quote a cargo-space figure with the standard 60/40 split-folding rear seats folded, but the releases inside the trunk make them easy to fold.


## Technology


6/10


A standard digital instrument cluster measures 8 inches in most trim levels, with the SEL upgrading to a larger 10.25-inch display and expanded functionality. In addition to improved graphics, the larger display offers full configurability, more data panels, and the ability to show full-screen navigation.


To the right, the Jetta has an 8-inch infotainment touchscreen with a thick frame containing touch-sensing menu shortcuts and control knobs. The screen and controls are further surrounded by another thick frame of black plastic, which makes the display look larger and more sophisticated than it is.


Standard features include wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto, SiriusXM 360L satellite radio, voice control, and six stereo speakers. Wireless smartphone charging is standard from the Sport trim, and the SEL upgrades to a navigation system and an eight-speaker Volkswagen Premium Audio system.


Several connected services plans are available. They include Remote Access (remote engine start, teen driver alerts, remote vehicle access); Safe & Secure (automatic-collision notification, SOS emergency assistance, stolen vehicle tracking, information assistance); and In-Vehicle Premium (Wi-Fi hotspot, natural voice recognition, text-to-speech messaging).


Our test car did not have an active subscription to In-Vehicle Premium, which was obvious from the first voice command we gave it: “Find the nearest Starbucks”. It couldn’t handle this, even when simplifying to “Find Starbucks” or following the instructions on the touchscreen display, but Apple CarPlay and Android Auto integration mean drivers don’t have to rely on it.


Also, the infotainment system’s user interface leaves something to be desired. Choose the Nav shortcut, and instead of getting a map, drivers get a mostly dark screen, the purpose of which is a mystery. And VW makes it very hard to understand what users must do to access the map.


Similarly, to adjust the safety-feature settings, the Assist Systems menu tile opens a pleasant graphic that is not at all what drivers want to see. To access the menus allowing modification of the settings, users must find the little icon in the lower corner of the screen and touch it. Why is that extra step required?


Lastly, the driver-assistance menus in the infotainment system and in the digital instrumentation overlap but don’t exactly match one another. Some settings are available in one location or the other. Good luck remembering where.


## Safety


8/10


Every 2027 Jetta has IQ.Drive, Volkswagen’s collection of driver-assistance features. It includes forward-collision warning with pedestrian detection, automatic emergency braking, Travel Assist (adaptive cruise control with lane-centering assist), lane-departure warning, lane-keep assist, Emergency Assist (automatically brakes to a stop if the driver becomes unresponsive), and high-beam assist.


Additionally, the Jetta has active blind-spot monitors with steering assist, rear cross-traffic alert, and an automatic post-collision braking system, but these features aren’t marketed as part of IQ.Drive.


The driver-assistance tech consistently impressed us with its accuracy, smoothness, and refinement. Travel Assist responded naturally when other vehicles would cut into the gap ahead. Some similar systems prioritize distance management over how a human driver would usually respond in such a situation, leading to unnecessarily abrupt braking. The Jetta handles these situations in a far more refined manner.


Aside from some inconsistency in how the car responded when accelerating back up to speed after slower vehicles exited the highway, Travel Assist worked exceptionally well. We also like that drivers can choose a lane-departure warning vibration issued through the steering wheel. And while the wheel doesn’t have hands-on sensing, the need to make small inputs to signify that we were paying attention wasn’t as tiresome as it is in other cars.


The 2027 Jetta has mostly favorable crash test ratings. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration gave it an overall rating of five out of five stars, but digging a little deeper, it earned four-star ratings for driver and front passenger protection in a frontal-impact collision.


Insurance Institute for Highway Safety (IIHS) ratings included Good for performance in the small overlap and updated moderate overlap frontal-impact tests, but a lower Acceptable rating in the updated side-impact test. Headlights and pedestrian front-crash prevention tech both rated Marginal. These scores weren’t good enough to earn the Jetta an IIHS Top Safety Pick award.


## Cost-effectiveness


7/10


While the Jetta’s price range is appealing, Volkswagen doesn’t offer a fuel-saving hybrid powertrain option, which buyers can get in the Honda Civic, the Hyundai Elantra, and the Toyota Corolla. Most rivals offer a superior powertrain warranty, some have more generous trial subscriptions to connected services, and a couple are available with AWD.


Nevertheless, the Jetta’s cost-effectiveness improves slightly in 2027 because two of its primary rivals have reduced their complimentary scheduled maintenance programs, leaving the Jetta with a comparatively appealing Carefree Maintenance plan that includes no-charge 10,000-mile and 20,000-mile service visits or complimentary service for two years, whichever comes first.


Overall, the 2027 Volkswagen Jetta is a competitive alternative to the sales leaders in the compact-car class. It is most satisfying to drive on longer highway trips, where it returns surprisingly good fuel economy, but it’s still worth it if drivers decide to take the long way home.
